# Virtual Threads

Virtual threads, final in Java 21 through
[JEP 444](https://openjdk.org/jeps/444), are ordinary `Thread` instances
scheduled by the Java runtime. They suit many independent tasks that spend most
of their time blocked, commonly on I/O. They do not make CPU-bound work faster,
remove shared-state coordination, or increase the capacity of databases and
other downstream services.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- distinguish a platform thread, a virtual thread, and a carrier thread, and
  explain which scheduler owns each decision;
- select virtual threads for numerous independent, predominantly blocking tasks
  and reject them as a CPU-parallelism optimisation;
- explain that a virtual thread is still a `Thread`, including its daemon
  lifecycle and the need to await work whose completion matters; and
- distinguish Java 21-era monitor pinning from Java 24’s improved monitor
  behaviour, and use the appropriate JDK diagnostic when investigating
  remaining pinning.

## Prerequisite

Install an
[Oracle Java 21](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java21)
JDK or newer and ensure `java` and `javac` resolve to it in the terminal.

## The program to inspect

### Platform threads, virtual threads, and carriers

A platform thread is typically a one-to-one wrapper around an operating-system
thread. The operating system schedules it, and it remains associated with that
OS thread for its lifetime. A platform thread is suitable for all work, but its
OS-managed stack and resources make it comparatively expensive to create in
very large numbers.

A virtual thread is also an instance of `java.lang.Thread`, but the Java runtime
schedules it. It is not permanently associated with an OS thread. To execute,
the runtime mounts the virtual thread on a platform thread called a *carrier*.
When a virtual thread performs a supported blocking operation, the runtime can
unmount it; its carrier is then available to run a different virtual thread.

```text
Java runtime scheduler
  carrier (platform thread) ── mounts ──> virtual thread A runs
  carrier (platform thread) <── unmount ─ virtual thread A blocks for I/O
  carrier (platform thread) ── mounts ──> virtual thread B runs
```

The carrier is an implementation detail, not the thread visible to application
code. `Thread.currentThread()` in a virtual-thread task returns that virtual
thread, not its carrier. Do not infer the number or identity of carriers from
log output, thread names, or a local run; carrier scheduling is neither a JMM
guarantee nor an application-level execution policy.

Every virtual thread is a daemon thread. Unlike a live non-daemon platform
thread, it does not keep the JVM running. Code that requires virtual-thread work
to finish must therefore join the thread or give that lifecycle responsibility
to another explicit owner; creating the thread is not sufficient.

### Independent blocking tasks

Each request starts as a virtual thread with an explicit name, confirms its own
logical thread identity, and blocks briefly. The program joins every thread
because virtual threads are daemon threads: without another non-daemon thread,
the JVM may begin shutdown before their work completes.

The JMM connection is `Thread.join()`: all actions in a thread happen-before a
successful return from `join()` in another thread. The output does not establish
a carrier assignment, scheduling, visibility, or performance guarantee; it only
reports the program’s explicit lifecycle management and each task’s identity.

```java
public final class Main {

    public static void main(final String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        logHeaderAndJavaVersion("Virtual Threads");

        final List<Thread> requests = List.of(
                startBlockingRequest("request-1"),
                startBlockingRequest("request-2"),
                startBlockingRequest("request-3"));

        log("Started " + requests.size() + " virtual threads for independent blocking requests.");
        waitForAllThreadsToComplete(requests);
        log("All requests completed.");

        PinnedVirtualThread.run();
        log("Pinned-task diagnostic completed.");
    }

    private static Thread startBlockingRequest(final String name) {
        return Thread.ofVirtual()
                .name(name)
                .start(() -> {
                    log("The request runs as a virtual thread: " + Thread.currentThread().isVirtual());
                    Threads.sleepForAFewMilliseconds();
                });
    }

    private Main() {}
}
```

### Pinning is a diagnostic concern

A virtual thread normally unmounts from its carrier while blocked, allowing the
carrier to run another virtual thread. In JDK 21 through JDK 23, a virtual
thread that blocked while executing `synchronized` code was pinned to its
carrier. Pinning did not make the program incorrect, but frequent, long-lived
pinning could reduce scalability.

This deliberately small case reproduces that Java 21 diagnostic. JDK 24
delivered [JEP 491](https://openjdk.org/jeps/491), so blocking while holding a
monitor no longer pins a virtual thread in current JDKs. Do not replace
`synchronized` solely because of virtual threads; choose a locking mechanism
based on the coordination problem being solved.

```java
final class PinnedVirtualThread {

    private static final Duration BLOCKING_TIME = Duration.ofMillis(100);

    static void run() throws InterruptedException {
        final Object monitor = new Object();
        final Thread thread = Thread.ofVirtual()
                .name("pinned-blocking-task")
                .start(() -> blockWhileHolding(monitor));
        thread.join();
    }

    private static void blockWhileHolding(final Object monitor) {
        synchronized (monitor) {
            try {
                Thread.sleep(BLOCKING_TIME);
            } catch (final InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
                throw new IllegalStateException("Pinned task was interrupted", e);
            }
        }
    }

    private PinnedVirtualThread() {}
}
```

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from this example directory. Choose one of the following ways
to run the example.

1. Run the example using the
   [Maven `exec` plugin](https://www.mojohaus.org/exec-maven-plugin/).

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean compile exec:exec
   ```

   One possible run; thread ordering will vary.

   ```
   ...

   [12:34:56.805] [   VirtualThread[#23,request-3]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3] The request runs as a virtual thread: true

   [12:34:57.316] [                                          Thread[#1,main,5,main]] All requests completed.
   [12:34:57.418] [                                          Thread[#1,main,5,main]] Pinned-task diagnostic completed.
   ...
   ```

2. Build the application and create the JAR file.

   Build the executable JAR and run the historical monitor-pinning diagnostic.
   The `jdk.tracePinnedThreads` property is a JDK 21 diagnostic: its stack trace
   shows that the virtual thread blocked while holding a monitor. It is not a
   JMM guarantee or a performance measurement. JDK 24 and later implement
   [JEP 491](https://openjdk.org/jeps/491), so this command does not report
   monitor pinning there.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) List the created JAR file.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name './target/libs'
   ```

   The application JAR file

   ```
   ./target/libs
   └── virtual-threads-1.0.0.jar

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

   Run the application.

   ```shell
   java \
     -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full \
     --module-path './target/libs' \
     --module demo
   ```

   One possible run; thread ordering will vary.
